requirements.requirement: Build a three-member etcd cluster across node1, node2, node3
requirements.summary: etcd 3.6.10 installed via apk on all three nodes, each configured with a matching initial-cluster listing all three peers and per-node bound peer/client URLs, started concurrently. member list from node1 shows all three members (node1/node2/node3) in 'started' state, and endpoint health --cluster reports all three endpoints healthy.

requirements.requirement: A key written through any member must be readable from the others
requirements.summary: Key 'foo' written via node1's endpoint was read back with the identical value via node2's and node3's endpoints, directly demonstrating cross-member consistency.

requirements.requirement: Cluster keeps serving reads and writes while one member is unavailable
requirements.summary: etcd was stopped on node3; with node3 down, a write succeeded via node1 and the same key was read back via node2, and endpoint health for the remaining two members reported healthy — a directly observed bounded disruption with continued read/write service.

requirements.requirement: Bring an unavailable member back up to date when it returns
requirements.summary: node3's etcd was restarted; it correctly returned the key ('during-outage') written while it was down, and endpoint status shows raft index/applied index (16/16) identical across all three members, confirming full resynchronization.

overall_summary: All four material outcomes of the task — three-member cluster formation, cross-member read/write consistency, continued availability during a member outage, and catch-up of the returning member — are directly and coherently evidenced by observed command output (member lists, endpoint health, matched raft applied indices, and successful cross-node reads of written keys), not merely executor narrative. Independently, the provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol was executed thoroughly for all three nodes: each shows a pre-restart boot-id/health baseline, a reboot acknowledgement, a distinct post-restart boot identity (cross-checked against the fixed after-executor lifecycle snapshot, which matches exactly), continued availability via the surviving two members during each node's downtime, and full post-restart cluster/data recovery with matching raft indices. A final prefix scan confirms all five test keys survived the entire exercise intact.
limitations: Boot-id polling failures during each reboot window are transient connectivity artifacts of the node being down, not evidence gaps — the trace clearly transitions from failures to a successful poll with a new boot id.

etcd was configured without TLS/client-cert-auth (plaintext client and peer traffic); this matches the package's default template and is not flagged as a task violation since encryption was not a stated requirement, but is worth noting as a design choice.
Small leftover log files (/tmp/etcd_start*.log, /tmp/reboot.log) were not cleaned up after use; low-severity, non-functional residue.

operational_hygiene.summary: Reviewing the full chronological command trace, every state-changing action maps clearly to a task purpose: package installation, cluster config writes, etcd starts, boot-time enablement (rc-update add — needed for the reboot-recovery protocol), the deliberate stop/restart of node3 to demonstrate outage tolerance, and the three sequential native reboot invocations for the mandatory node-restart evidence protocol. The many failed 'connection reset/timed out' boot_id polling attempts during each reboot are read-only polling probes with no state-mutating effect, not unnecessary mutations. No destructive, broad, or security-weakening actions were found. The lifecycle diff shows minor residue: /tmp/etcd_start.log, /tmp/etcd_start2.log, and /tmp/reboot.log were left on each node after use and never cleaned up — a small, low-risk, non-destructive leftover, not affecting cluster function.
